# caliper-docgen-vite-plugin

A Vite plugin that exposes your React components' props on a virtual module and updates it through HMR as you edit.

```bash
npm install --save-dev caliper-docgen-vite-plugin
```

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vite'
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react'
import { caliperDocgen } from 'caliper-docgen-vite-plugin'

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react(), caliperDocgen({ srcDirs: ['src'] })],
})
```

```ts
import docgen from 'virtual:caliper-docgen'

// A component lists the ids of its prop sets; a prop set maps each prop name to a prop id, and each distinct prop is
// written once, in `docgen.props`.
const [firstSetId] = docgen.components['Button'].props
const label = docgen.props[docgen.propSets[firstSetId].label]
```

On every change the virtual module reloads with the same output a fresh extraction would give, including removed components, enums and diagnostics. To apply changes yourself, listen for the update event:

```ts
import.meta.hot?.on(
  'caliper-docgen:update',
  ({ updatedKeys, updatedComponents, props, removedKeys, diagnostics, removedDiagnostics }) => {
    // Events arrive in revision order, each a delta from the one before: delete removedKeys, set updatedKeys[i] to
    // updatedComponents[i], merge props, propSets and nameLists into the tables of the same names, drop removedDiagnostics and add diagnostics. Props no
    // component refers to any more can be dropped.
  },
)
```

A change to a tsconfig, `package.json` or lockfile in or above `srcDirs` (installing a package, editing `paths`) re-extracts everything and arrives as an ordinary update event.

Pass `cache: false` to read and write none of the on-disk caches under `node_modules/.cache`; the output is the same. Types your props import from installed packages are resolved by default; pass `loadDependencies: false` to leave them as named references. `htmlAttributes: 'curated' | 'full' | 'none'` chooses which HTML attributes a component inherits from its element to list (`skipHtmlProps` is `'none'`).

Extraction diagnostics are logged once each: errors and warnings by default. `logLevel: 'error' | 'warn' | 'info' | 'silent'` changes that, and `onDiagnostic(diagnostic)` receives every one.

In `vite build --watch`, a change to any file under `srcDirs`, or to that configuration, triggers a rebuild, even one no bundle module imports. A build fails if extraction fails.

## Storybook without the docgen server

On Storybook 10, or Storybook 11 with `features.docgenServer: false`, Storybook reads each component's `__docgenInfo`. With `injectDocgenInfo`, the plugin assigns it from the session, in react-docgen-typescript's shape, and an edit re-transforms every module whose components it changed. Turn off Storybook's own docgen plugin so it doesn't overwrite the assignments:

```ts
// .storybook/main.ts
import type { StorybookConfig } from '@storybook/react-vite'
import { caliperDocgen } from 'caliper-docgen-vite-plugin'

const config: StorybookConfig = {
  framework: '@storybook/react-vite',
  stories: ['../src/**/*.stories.tsx'],
  typescript: { reactDocgen: false },
  viteFinal: (config) => ({
    ...config,
    plugins: [...(config.plugins ?? []), caliperDocgen({ srcDirs: ['src'], injectDocgenInfo: true })],
  }),
}
export default config
```

Each assignment sits in a `try`, so a component the module can't reach by name (an anonymous default export) keeps no docs instead of failing. On Storybook 11 with the docgen server on, use `caliper-docgen-storybook` instead.

Extraction runs on OXC through [`caliper-docgen-napi`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/caliper-docgen-napi), so a single-file update takes about 2ms. Requires Vite 7 or 8. The module uses the canonical output format, not the `react-docgen-typescript` shape.

Docs and benchmarks: [orin-dx.com/tools/caliper](https://orin-dx.com/tools/caliper/). Source: [github.com/orin-dx/caliper](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper).

## License

FSL-1.1-MIT. Each version becomes MIT two years after its release.

Each `parse_file()` call gets its own OXC allocator. No AST node escapes the function — all extracted data is owned, heap-allocated types. This is what makes the rayon parallelism safe.

The watch path reuses analysis across file changes. A single-file update calls `parse_file()` on the changed file and re-resolves only the affected components.

`WatchSession` publishes one immutable `Revision` at a time: global source data, the named-type index, resolved components with their recorded dependencies, diagnostics and the assembled output. An update builds the next revision off to the side and publishes it with one atomic store, so a reader sees one complete revision. Cold extraction and watch revisions share `Revision::assemble()`, and a watch snapshot equals a cold extract of the same files (see `docs/architecture/pipeline-orchestration.md`).

Between parse and resolve, the declarations of installed packages that project types name are loaded by name into a shared `DependencyLayer` (`dependency_types.rs`, on by default; ADR 0010). A lazy session (`WatchSession::lazy`, ADR 0016) parses and indexes every file but resolves a component only when a request names it, which is how the Storybook addon runs; every answer equals the batch extraction's for the same key. A session can also ask a warm TypeScript 7.1 checker for the requested component (`semanticTypes: 'on-demand'`, ADR 0022), experimental and off by default.

## Crate and package graph

```mermaid
graph TD
    core["crates/core\ncaliper-docgen-core\nExtraction and resolution — file I/O, no async"]
    binding["crates/binding\ncaliper-docgen-napi\nNAPI + tokio runtime"]
    cli["crates/cli\ncaliper-docgen\nCLI binary"]
    semantic["crates/semantic\ncaliper-docgen-semantic\nExperimental TS 7.1 backend"]
## Design decisions

### OXC instead of the TypeScript compiler

`react-docgen-typescript` creates a TypeScript `Program` — this loads all imported types transitively, runs type inference, and is single-threaded. `caliper-docgen` parses each file independently in parallel with no type-checking pass. The trade-off: TypeScript-only semantics (conditional types, `infer`, deep utility type evaluation) fall through to `{ kind: "opaque" }`. Everything structurally expressible — interfaces, intersections, unions, `Omit`, `Pick`, `VariantProps` — resolves correctly.

### `FxHashMap` over `HashMap`

OXC uses `FxHashMap` throughout. For short keys (type names, file paths) the FNV-derived hash in `rustc-hash` is faster than SipHash with no DoS-relevant surface for this use case.

### `CompactString` for type and prop names
## Crate guide

- `crates/core` — pure extraction logic; @crates/core/AGENTS.md
- `crates/cli` — clap CLI, no logic; @crates/cli/AGENTS.md
- `crates/binding` — thin NAPI wrapper, delegates to core
- `crates/semantic` — opt-in TypeScript 7.1 checker backend (`docs/type-checker-integration.md`)
- `crates/tsc-client` — client for the checker process the semantic crate drives

## Scripts

No new sh, py or mjs script unless a CI job, the weekly or a documented recipe calls it; prefer a Rust test or the existing oracle TypeScript. A measurement run once is recorded in docs (`docs/measurement.md`, `docs/gate-measurements.md`), not committed as a script. Each script's caller is listed in `docs/measurement.md`.

## The checker lane

ADR 0026's gate before the default flips: the suite through the checker path (`--experimental-semantic-types` with the pinned `tsrs`, and `--no-resolver-facts`, so a default and a union's member order come from the checker and oxc's syntax, not the structural resolver), held to `checker-expectations.json`, which has the shape of `expectations.json`. Green rows must stay green; every other row is a documented gap with a one-line reason. The lane fails when a row is better or worse than its entry (an improvement means the gap closed: update the entry and drop the `gap`), when the checker did not answer for a row, or when the backend was unavailable.

```sh
just test-checker-lane   # CI job "Test / Checker lane"
```

## Known gaps (cross-referenced, not re-derived)

These are documented elsewhere and intentionally not re-litigated here:

- **Generic substitution through nested builtin chains** (Ariakit `Props<T, O>` and 5 siblings) — `docs/benchmarks.md`, "Corsa-deferred" generic-parameter-substitution item.
- **`composes` as a stop-gap, not a fix** — `docs/benchmarks.md` explains `composes` population closes the _symptom_ (silent zero-props output) for type-checker-boundary failures, not the underlying inability to expand conditional/mapped/indexed-access types without a real checker.
- **Resolver precedence's two residual divergences** between `chain.rs` and `named.rs` (React-builtin-check ordering, `is_ts_utility_type` check ordering) — not covered by the shared precedence above.
- **The type of a value built by a call** (`z.infer<typeof schema>` with `const schema = z.object({ ... })`; a store, a hook's result). `typeof X` is a type here only for components, cva variants and `as const` arrays (and now `declare const X: readonly [...]`). TypeScript infers the call's generic arguments from its argument expression and then evaluates the library's conditional and mapped types; that needs the checker (ADR 0006), so the prop stays a named reference (`Event["name"]`) with an Info `OPAQUE_TYPE` diagnostic whose help names the remedy: declare the type where it is used, or `--experimental-semantic-types`. shadcn's `CopyButton.event` is the example.

15:- `session_component_answers(session_id, keys) -> String` — `{ key: { docgenInfo, diagnostics } }` for each requested component, each diagnostic with `affects` set to the key; a key the session lacks is left out. A lazy session resolves each requested component now, in parallel, so a host learns whether a component's props may be incomplete from the same call that returns them. With `semanticTypes: 'on-demand'` the session asks the warm TypeScript 7.1 checker for the component first and waits up to `semanticWaitMs` (default 150), or `semanticWaitEmptyMs` (default 2000) when the structural answer lists no props, before taking the structural answer (ADR 0022). Synchronous, with `contain_panic` directly.
45:**Invariant 3: `JsExtractOptions` carries only options the pipeline reads.** Every field of `JsExtractOptions` maps to a `PipelineOptions` field or is consumed by the binding itself when it builds a session (`lazy`, `semanticTypes`, `tscPath`, `semanticWaitMs`, `semanticWaitEmptyMs`). There are no JSON-string fields for map-valued options: no `extraPathsJson` or `knownTypeOverridesJson` exists, and neither `extraPaths` nor `knownTypeOverrides` is an option anywhere. Adding an option means adding the field here, mapping it in `TryFrom<JsExtractOptions> for PipelineOptions`, and a test that shows it changes output; an option that is accepted but not read lets a caller believe it is honored.

# Performance

How fast Caliper is and what it costs is recorded in `docs/measurement.md`: a weekly run on five pinned corpora, and `just bench` for a change that touches the resolver. The criterion benches (`cargo bench -p caliper-docgen-core`) and `docs/benchmarks.md` cover single fixtures. This page keeps the measurements that explain where the time goes.

The per-pull-request scorecard that used to enforce these numbers is gone. It caught one real regression (Mantine 38% and Chakra 47% slower after a batch of 20 resolver pull requests merged on 2026-10-26, found by the weekly run), and its gates failed on runner noise and on bases that had moved. The figures below came from it and are history, not limits.

## Size model

Extraction time fits t ≈ 6.4 ms + 0.13 ms/kLOC + 3.8 ms/kprop (props summed over components). It is a sizing guide, reported by the old scorecard as "Model ms", never a gate: a fixed cost that varies by machine dominates small corpora, so per-corpus residuals vary too much to gate on. On the run below the model is within 2× of the measured extract time on every corpus (0.45× for mantine to 1.6× for chakra).

## Results, 2026-10-22


This report has two independent halves: **performance** (how fast) and **output quality** (how correct/complete). They're measured differently on purpose — a fast tool that produces wrong output isn't actually useful, and this project's whole premise is "faster AND at least as accurate," so both get held to a real, reproducible standard here. The Rust-internal numbers reproduce with `crates/core/benches/`; the cross-tool ones were produced by the removed harness, and the weekly record replaces them — see [Reproducing these numbers](#reproducing-these-numbers).

## Tools compared

| Tool                      | Version   | Approach                                         |
| ------------------------- | --------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `caliper-docgen`          | this repo | OXC parser, no type-checking pass                |
| `react-docgen-typescript` | 2.2.2     | full `ts.Program` + real TypeScript type checker |
| `react-docgen`            | 7.1.1     | Babel AST walk, weak native TS support           |


### TypeScript's checker as the oracle

RDT has mistakes of its own. With `--oracle` the run also asks TypeScript 7.1's checker (`apps/oracle/src/oracle.ts`, `typescript-beta/sync`, the `7.1.0-beta` package) for each prop's type and compares it structurally with Caliper's canonical `--json`, extracted with `--html-attributes full --include-unexported --load-dependencies --collapse-inherited-props none`. The weekly table shows the share of props that agree (identical, or the same type spelled by name) and the share the checker contradicts, for Caliper, RDT and react-docgen, and the headline below. `agree` is the loose number; `wrong` is the one that matters and the one the weekly issue gates on, but the comparator has artifacts that make it both over- and under-report. `docs/rdt-differences.md` lists every class of disagreement with an example, how it is counted and whether the comparator scored it right. The checker is a beta and the backend that uses it is an opt-in (`docs/type-checker-integration.md`), so a disagreement is a reason to look, not a verdict on its own.

| Verdict | Meaning |
| --- | --- |

# 0001. Parse with OXC instead of the TypeScript compiler

**Status:** Accepted **Date:** 2026-07-22 (retroactive — true since the project started)

## Context

# 0006. Run the TypeScript backend as a second resolver, not a leaf patcher

**Status:** Accepted, feature-gating superseded by 0007, superseded in part by 0026 **Date:** 2026-09-26

**Note (2026-11-02):** `ExtractionOutput` has had a `schemaVersion` since ADR 0017, so the last Consequences bullet no longer applies to it. "Stays free of I/O" means no compiler process: `crates/core` reads and writes files itself (discovery, module resolution, the caches) and spawns nothing.

# 0022. Ask a warm checker for the requested component

**Status:** Accepted **Date:** 2026-10-26 **Amended:** 2026-11-11 (a component the structural pass lists no props for waits up to `semanticWaitEmptyMs`, default 2000; one request in flight per component and file version, joined by later callers; interactive requests before background ones; the addon asks for the opening story when `storybook dev` starts)

## Context

## Index

One line per ADR, with what it guards. Add a line when you add an ADR.

- [1. Parse with OXC instead of the TypeScript compiler](0001-oxc-over-typescript-compiler.md) — do not add a type-checking pass to the default path. The opt-in backend is 0006.
- [2. Hand-write Serialize/Deserialize for PropType instead of deriving it](0002-manual-serialize-for-prop-type.md) — do not derive them on `PropType` or `CollectedType`.
- [3. Cache the DTS parse cache with positional (not named) MessagePack](0003-positional-msgpack-cache-encoding.md) — do not reorder, insert or remove `SourceData` fields without bumping `CACHE_SCHEMA_VERSION`.
- 4. Defer full type-checker integration — removed: superseded by 0006. The gap list and gates are in `docs/type-checker-integration.md`.
30:- [22. Ask a warm checker for the requested component](0022-ask-a-warm-checker-for-the-requested-component.md) — do not route by predicted risk or check the whole project to answer one story: ask the TypeScript checker for the component a request names, wait a bounded time, and take the structural answer when it is slower. Extends 0007's runtime opt-in from a project run to a session.
34:- [26. The checker is the type authority; oxc supplies syntax](0026-the-checker-is-the-type-authority.md) — Accepted. Do not make a type decision in a projection, key a cache on a checker type id, or bump the pinned tsrs without the construct suite and a parity run against the Go checker: the checker gives the prop set, types, requiredness and descriptions, oxc the candidates, defaults, positions and declaration order, and the structural resolver is only the fallback. Supersedes in part 0006 and 0007.

# Migrating from react-docgen-typescript

`caliper-docgen` targets output-shape compatibility with `react-docgen-typescript` (RDT) via the CLI's `--format rdt` flag. The NAPI binding and Vite plugin's virtual module expose this tool's own canonical format (`kind`-tagged `PropType`, shown in the main README). For RDT's shape at that layer, a NAPI session returns each component's `__docgenInfo`, and the Vite plugin's `injectDocgenInfo` option assigns it.

This document covers what's compatible today, what's intentionally different, and what's a known gap rather than a design choice.

## Should you switch today?

Output should match closely if your components use:

- Plain interfaces or type aliases
- `forwardRef` (including wrapped in an `as` cast), `FC`, or HOC wrapping

The built-in TypeScript checker now answers by default (ADR 0026). `extract`, `check` and `inspect` merge its answer over the structural one, prop by prop, and wait for it. A native session and the Storybook addon ask it for each component a request names, and still show the structural props first when it is slower than `semanticWaitMs` (150 ms). `--no-checker`, or `checker: false` in `docgen.config.ts`, the native options or the addon's options, runs the structural resolver alone, as before. `watch`, `extractAll` and the Vite plugin stay structural.

The checker costs time and memory. `extract` of an app with 938 Chakra UI and MUI components takes about 6 s and 970 MiB, against 0.1 s and 200 MiB with `--no-checker`. A session that answered every one of them peaks at about 1 GB, against 380 MiB without the checker: each answer the session keeps now shares its props with the others, where before each kept its own copy, about 6.7 MiB per Chakra component.

Breaking: `--experimental-semantic-types`, the config's `experimentalSemanticTypes` and the `semanticTypes` option of the native binding and the Storybook addon are removed. The CLI and the config reject the old names as unknown, and the addon rejects `semanticTypes` by name. `PipelineOptions::experimental_semantic_types` is now `PipelineOptions::checker`, and it is `true` by default.

Action: drop `--experimental-semantic-types`, `experimentalSemanticTypes: true` and `semanticTypes: 'on-demand'`, since the checker now runs without them. Replace `semanticTypes: 'off'`, or a run that relied on the old structural default, with `checker: false` or `--no-checker`.
